title: 6.5 Overtraining Definition, Prevalence, Diagnosis, and Potential Markers

cards.front: What is the overtraining continuum, and how do functional overreaching (FOR), nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR), and overtraining syndrome (OTS) differ in recovery timeline?
cards.back:
Overtraining exists on a continuum driven by intensified training without adequate rest:
  • Functional Overreaching (FOR): Short-term performance dip followed by supercompensation recovery in days to weeks.
  • Nonfunctional Overreaching (NFOR): Performance stagnation or drop requiring weeks to months of recovery.
  • Overtraining Syndrome (OTS): Severe neuroendocrine and performance collapse requiring months to over a year of recovery.

cards.front: What is the estimated prevalence of overtraining syndrome among endurance athletes, and what is its primary physiological cause?
cards.back: Approximately 10% (7% to 21%) of collegiate swimmers and aerobic endurance athletes experience NFOR or OTS. The primary cause is an imbalance between heavy training loads and insufficient rest/recovery.

cards.front: How do heart rate variability (HRV), resting heart rate, and maximal heart rate respond to overtraining syndrome?
cards.back: HRV decreases with onset of OTS (indicating reduced parasympathetic tone or excessive sympathetic stimulation). Exercise-induced maximal heart rate decreases, while resting heart rate can either increase or decrease.

cards.front: How does increased training intensity vs. volume affect resting blood pressure during overreaching?
cards.back: Increased training volume generally does not affect resting blood pressure. However, increased training intensity can elevate resting diastolic blood pressure without altering resting systolic pressure.

cards.front: What alterations in serum creatine kinase (CK), blood lactate, and muscle glycogen accompany high-volume overtraining?
cards.back: High training volume increases creatine kinase (CK) levels (indicating muscle tissue microtrauma). Muscle glycogen stores decrease, contributing to lowered submaximal blood lactate concentrations.

cards.front: How does the free testosterone-to-cortisol ratio change during volume overtraining, and what shift marks potential OTS?
cards.back: The free testosterone-to-cortisol ratio decreases or stays the same with increased volume. A decrease of 30% or more in the free testosterone-to-cortisol ratio serves as a potential marker for OTS.

cards.front: What endocrine dysfunction underlies decreased growth hormone secretion in overtrained athletes?
cards.back: Decreased growth hormone secretion and altered neuroendocrine responses during overtraining stem primarily from impaired hypothalamic function, rather than intrinsic pituitary gland failure.

cards.front: How do catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine) alter during volume overtraining, and what characterizes parasympathetic OTS?
cards.back: Severe volume overtraining reduces basal dopamine levels and drops nocturnal epinephrine levels. In advanced cases, endurance athletes exhibit parasympathetic OTS, characterized by blunted catecholamine sensitivity and autonomic fatigue.

cards.front: How is detraining defined, and how does it differ from a pre-competition taper?
cards.back:
• Detraining: Partial or complete loss of training adaptations due to insufficient training stimulus, governed by the principle of reversibility.
  • Tapering: A planned, strategic reduction in training volume (duration/frequency) with maintained intensity designed to optimize performance.

cards.front: How much does maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) decline during short-term vs. long-term detraining, and what drives this loss?
cards.back: Maximal oxygen uptake drops 4% to 14% during short-term detraining (≤4 weeks) and 6% to 20% during long-term detraining (>4 weeks). This decline is driven by plasma volume contraction, decreased stroke volume, lower maximal cardiac output, and loss of oxidative enzyme activity.
